episodes.d: Who Checks the Builder. Why the person who builds a thing is the worst person to test it, why the checker must not share the builder's goal, and how to make it safe to say 'show me' before the rain does it for you.

For three years Dr Non wrote perfect policy for people he had never met. Why the corner office feels like progress, what Hayek, Jane Jacobs and James C. Scott already knew about the view from above, the Four Ps (purpose, practicality, proof, people), and one five-minute habit for tomorrow: meet them first.
What does it cost to keep a checkable flood map alive under surge without inventing calm? Running FloodDash, from the inside.

episodes.t: 43. Home Is Where the Heart Is
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. A few years ago I was sitting at a bar inside the American Airlines terminal at Los Angeles airport, eating a Californian pizza, with both my phone and my laptop dying and no outlet anywhere near me. Nothing to read, nothing to answer. And for the first time in months I had to sit with my own thoughts about where I actually lived.

Coffee in hand. I once sat in an airport boarding area waiting for the first trip in years that was not for work. No presentation to prepare, no transcript, no meetings. And with nothing to prepare, I started making a list of everything I have never been.

Coffee in hand. Years ago I sat down alone at a hot pot restaurant in Bangkok on a weekday afternoon. Almost nobody else was there, so every waiter in the place ended up working for my one table, carrying plate after plate of raw meat over so I could cook it in front of me. And sitting there, watching them walk back and forth for me, I worked something out that I have used ever since.

episodes.t: 40. What a Man Is Supposed to Have
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. About a kilometre from where I did my fieldwork in Shanghai there is a park that turns into a marriage market every Sunday. Parents stand there holding their children's details written out on paper. Age. Income. And above all, whether there is an apartment. I used to walk past it after a week of interviews in the lanes, and it took me a long time to stop finding it strange.

Coffee in hand. The first time somebody in Shanghai asked me where I lived, I thought it was small talk. A retired factory worker at the gate of an old rowhouse compound, thermos of green tea welded to his hand, wanted to know which room, in which house, on which lane. Then whether the window faced south. Then whether the kitchen was mine, or shared. It took me weeks to work out that he was not making conversation. He was reading me.

episodes.t: 38. Where You Go When It Gets Hard
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Thoreau went to the woods because he wished to live deliberately. I went to Shanghai. And I watched a great many people I knew arrive in that city and find religion, while I went looking for reasons instead.

episodes.t: On Being a Distribution, Not a Point
episodes.d: Nineteen recordings of one man do not converge on a true recording. They make a cloud with a middle nobody has ever heard. On why auditing yourself for authenticity is the wrong question, and what to ask instead.

episodes.t: On Simulation, and Why You Can Relax
episodes.d: One-month special. Why the simulation argument is probably right, three theories of why we might be in here, and why that is a reason to hold your life more lightly. Built from days 95 and 27 of 100 Days of Non.

Coffee in hand. Here is a question I could not put down after reading Harari: what makes two strangers, who have never met and know nothing whatsoever about each other, hate each other? That is a very large question, and I do not think it is a rhetorical one.

episodes.t: 36. The Post I Kept Not Writing
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. I owed this blog six more rules and I simply did not write them. I forgot. Freud had a word for the kind of forgetting that is quietly doing a job for you, and I think he was right about mine.

Coffee in hand. I once walked twenty-eight kilometres across Tokyo in a single day — Tsukiji, Ginza, the Imperial Palace, Roppongi, and finally Shibuya, just before the metro closed. I arrived with almost nothing in my hands. That walk taught me more about what I own than any amount of tidying ever has.

Coffee in hand — and today that is not a throwaway line. My father carried a tea flask to work every day of his working life and came home with it empty. I grew up watching a man run himself on one hot drink and a fixed routine. I did not inherit the tea. I inherited the ritual.

episodes.d: Philippe Coutinho: same left foot, different team grammar. Peak talent is not a portable file. Thailand Soccer Podcast teaser — Non-Philosophy.

episodes.d: Thailand Soccer Podcast teaser. First touch as ethics at speed.

episodes.d: Thailand Soccer Podcast teaser. After the whistle: reset, centre circle, finite courage.
Nostalgia as memory versus policy. Keep the parts list; refuse the throne.

Coffee in hand. The architect Louis Kahn said that good architecture ages beautifully. I read that line years ago and stopped. That is it. That is exactly how I would like to get old — not preserved, not fighting it, just aged the way a good building ages.
Pitch special. Why The Non-Philosophy Podcast exists — confession that becomes a tool, no affirmations, help yourself first.

episodes.t: 32. Six Things You Are Actually Chasing
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Think of a decision you made this year that you justified with a practical reason — the job, the move, the purchase. Now ask which need it was really serving. The practical reason is almost never the whole answer.

episodes.t: 31. Stability Is What Dead Things Have
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Ask yourself honestly whether you want your life to be more stable — and then ask what a perfectly stable week would actually contain. Same pattern, no surprise, nothing undetectable. That is the thing you said you wanted.

Coffee in hand. You fasten your seat belt without thinking about it. Somebody made you do that, and you almost certainly agree with them. So where exactly is the line where being made to do something stops being an insult to your freedom?

Coffee in hand. Think about the last time you felt a flash of something ugly when someone you love made a plan that did not include you. Not the argument that followed — just that first half-second. What exactly was it defending?

episodes.t: 28. Alone Is Not the Same as Lonely
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Tonight, turn off every light except one screen and sit with it. Somewhere in the first ten minutes you will find out which one you are actually in — loneliness, or solitude. They feel identical for about a minute and then they stop.

episodes.t: 27. The Question I Nearly Answered Too Fast
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. A graduate school sent me a questionnaire, and one question asked whether I would do my PhD again. Of course I would, I thought. What a stupid question. And then my hand stopped on the way to the submit button. That pause is the whole episode.

Coffee in hand. Think about the last piece of bad news that landed on you — the accusation, the cancelled plan, the thing that was not your fault. How long did it take you to start explaining yourself? And what would have happened if you had said nothing at all?

Coffee in hand. A warning before we start: this one is for adults, and I am not going to talk around it. Here is the question I want to put to you. You have been taught your whole life that love and sex belong together. Where did you learn that, and have you ever once checked whether it is true?

Coffee in hand. The thing that has shaped me the most was never one decision. It was years of small, boring repetition, most of it with nothing to show for it at the time. I want to make the case for that unglamorous kind of change, because it works better than almost anything else I have tried.

episodes.t: 24. Confidence Is Built by Failing, Full Stop
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Years ago I walked off a stage feeling like a dead man, in front of a real audience, after a talk that genuinely fell apart. I want to tell you exactly what I did in the days after that — because that failure, not any talk that went well, is where the actual confidence came from.

episodes.t: 23. Why Reading the News Isn't Good for You
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. I found out about a story the entire world had been watching for days, weeks after everyone else already knew how it ended. I felt no shame once I noticed something: I had lost nothing by being late. That is not a throwaway line. It is the whole argument.

episodes.t: 22. Would I Be Okay If This Were the Last Thing I Ever Posted
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Before I post anything, I ask myself one blunt question: would I be okay if this were the last thing I ever wrote? Not because I am feeling morbid. Because it is the fastest filter I know for whether something is actually worth saying, or whether I just want to be seen saying it.

Coffee in hand. Design thinking became a workshop format with coloured sticky notes on a wall. Underneath the sticky notes there is a real method — and the one step almost everyone quietly skips happens to be the only step that was ever actually difficult.

episodes.t: 19. Doing the Work, or Occupying the Position
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. From the outside, on an ordinary week, someone who is actually doing the work and someone who is merely occupying the position look completely identical. The difference only ever shows up on the one week that goes wrong.

Coffee in hand. Look at your real to-do list, not the polite version. I would bet at least half of what is on it was never assigned to you by anyone. It simply accumulated, and it will keep sitting there, uninspected, until somebody finally says its name out loud.

episodes.t: 17. Why Modesty Is Bad for Society
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Hiding what you are genuinely good at feels, from the inside, like humility. I want to make the case that it is closer to theft — that you are quietly taking something other people actually needed and putting it back in your own pocket.

episodes.t: 16. The Half-Second After Someone Criticises Your Work
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. There is a very specific half-second, right after someone criticises something you made, where every part of you goes straight to defending it. I want to talk about that half-second precisely — because whatever was said inside it is usually the only thing in the whole conversation actually worth hearing.

episodes.t: 12. Every Extra Sentence Is a Cost
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Every extra sentence you write is a tax you charge someone else, without ever asking their permission first. Most writing advice is just decoration sitting on top of that one fact. I want to show you the fact underneath the decoration.

episodes.t: 15. The Four Noble Truths as a Design Brief
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. The Four Noble Truths are, structurally, a design brief: name the suffering, find what causes it, define what its ending looks like, build the path there. It is two and a half thousand years old, and it is better organised than most briefs I have been handed this year.

Twelve hours stuck in an airport taught me something years of trying harder never did. Effort spent on the part of a system you do not control looks exactly like effort — and produces exactly nothing. I learned that the hard way, in a plastic chair, at three in the morning.

Coffee in hand. Somewhere in the last week you made a fast, confident, gut-level call, and you were almost certainly right. Somewhere else that same week, that exact same instinct was confidently, disastrously wrong — and in the moment, you had no way of knowing which one you were in.

Coffee in hand. A city is a physical place where strangers try to live together without killing each other. That is a real definition, not a joke, and it costs nothing to write. This episode is a handful of sentences exactly like it.

Coffee in hand. The last time something disappointed you, look again at where the disappointment actually came from. Not from what happened. You built something in your own head first, quietly, in advance — and then completely forgot that you had built it.

episodes.t: 9. Beauty Is Not in the Thing Itself
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Hume said beauty is no quality in things themselves — it lives only in the eye that looks at them. Fine. Then explain why some decisions are still, unmistakably, wrong. That contradiction is where this episode lives.

Coffee in hand. Think of the best thing that has ever happened in your career. Now sit with the uncomfortable second question: how much of that was actually you, and how much was just where you happened to be standing when the door opened? Most people never honestly answer that. I think you owe it to yourself to.

Coffee in hand. Look at whatever is open in front of you right now — a plan, a room, a draft. Now ask the question almost nobody asks first: not what is missing from it, but what could be taken away. That one flipped question is the entire episode.

Coffee in hand. Somewhere in your life there is a system that has never once failed — a process, a relationship, the way you have always done a particular job. You probably file that under good news. I want you to spend the next ten minutes considering it might mean the opposite: that the real test simply has not happened yet.

episodes.t: 5. Three Beliefs That Should Cancel Each Other Out
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. Three beliefs that ought to cancel each other out, and don't. People are not born broken. Almost nothing that happens to you is yours to control. And you are still, completely, responsible for what you make of it. Try holding all three at once for the next ten minutes and see what it does to the next setback you have.

episodes.t: The One Critic I Never Doubt
episodes.d: Coffee in hand. It is Mother's Day here in Thailand today. Think of the last piece of honest feedback that actually changed how you did something — not a compliment, the real kind, the kind that stung a little. Who said it to you? And why did you listen to that sentence from them, when you would have waved it off from almost anyone else?

episodes.d: An early Non-Philosophy episode: Writing Is the Thinking, Not Its Record.

Twelve stories on one question: what crosses a line, who decides, and who pays? Twenty attacks on Riyadh's airport in two weeks and a strike on Aden's palace, Trump rules out nuclear weapons on Iran, the IEA's 330 million barrels and the Hormuz harvest warning, a tense EU summit and a Lukoil waiver, school tragedies in Oregon and Peshawar, Istanbul's floods, Thailand's rain outlook for 21 to 25 October, 2,500 tonnes of e-waste in Rayong, Thailand and Cambodia's sea-boundary talks, a 121 billion baht investment push, and spyware delivered by ads.

Seventeen stories on one question: what actually holds when the weight arrives? A school roof collapses in Peshawar, Istanbul's heaviest rain in 84 years, a China–North Korea bridge that stood finished for twelve years, bleached corals rescued by touching a healthy twin, Bangkok's march on the IMF and World Bank meetings, two ships sunk in Hormuz and the fertiliser warning, Taiz under siege, Kyiv's grid and Starlink restored, Black Sea tankers, US troops and strikes in Latin America, and Costa Rica's mega-prison.

Starlink puts a speed limit on Ukraine's drones and nobody will say who set it. Thirteen stories on one question: who holds the switch? Bangladeshis trafficked to Russia's front line, the Nord Stream trial, a ship sunk in Hormuz and the fertiliser that cannot get out, rescue boats stopped by fuel prices, Mauritius riots over water, Albania's students, Kenya's second Ebola case, Indian workers training robots, Australia's algorithm off-switch, paid-for Michelin stars and the world's oldest shipwreck.

A hidden recorder wrapped in toilet paper at OpenAI, and a dozen stories on one question: who has the right to know? Kyiv hit with no early warning, drones sink a ship off NATO's Bulgarian coast, Russia arrests a Japanese reporter, Saudi-Houthi strikes and oil, Pope Leo's lung cancer, the Taliban switch off BBC FM, Indonesia's haze and a record El Niño, emergency rule in Imran Khan's stronghold, Joseph Kabila leads Congo rebels, China's paid companions, and why fluent AI translation hides its errors.

Ten stories, one question: who keeps the score? Trump's Ukraine energy ceasefire and the Russian diesel deal; Gen Syrskyi says Russia's advance is broken; Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport; backdated papers hide $672m of Abramovich assets; Batam residents vs data centres over water; a new flood in Nepal; India's Cockroach Janta Party at Jantar Mantar; the IMF meets in Bangkok; Microsoft's Brad Smith says milk is more regulated than AI, and a rogue AI agent's fake police tip; hackers heat French supermarket fridges to 50C.

A Nobel for a war-crimes judge, then sanctions on her court within hours. Plus 78 dead in two days in Ukraine, missiles over Riyadh's airport, and rain on Bangkok. Who keeps the score when the people with power decide the referee is the problem?
FloodDash Experience, episode three. A weather bulletin can be true and still teach nobody. How a flood map translates official fog into a named soi without inventing depth.

What every piece of the pipeline costs, why the check on the model matters more than the model, and the month Dr Non spent assuming the paid voice must be better without checking.

A Russian drone hit a train near Poland thirty minutes after Boris Johnson's diplomatic train cleared the corridor. Sweden hangs on about twenty thousand votes. Hormuz talks slip. Dr Non asks who is writing the timetable.
The White House pulled a Tetris-style “Build The Wall” game after The Tetris Company complained. Other parody games stayed up. Dr Non follows the IP invoice.

A special. Google just bought twenty-two years of a Finnish nuclear plant to feed its data centres, while this programme has made fifty-nine episodes on one laptop for nothing. What are you actually buying when you buy scale — and what does free really cost?

Five Iranian tankers burned; Brent hit $100. Trump ties the war's end to midterms. Dr Non follows the invoice from Hormuz to an IAEA referral, Google's Finnish nuclear deal, and a Ceuta warning that sat in a file.
Britain's foreign secretary told Parliament that settlers are cleansing Palestinians from parts of the West Bank. It shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
A Bangkok boy meets Shanghai before he knows the word lilong. Special on Locating Shanghai — gentrification from within, heritage as rent, and why a PhD lane still opens its gate.
Arm’s Rene Haas told the BBC AI will find a cancer cure in our lifetime. Dr Non separates the stock story from the data story.

An Italian privacy collective shut itself down after a US terrorism listing. Saxony-Anhalt handed the AfD forty-four percent. Same morning, Trump's envoys rode a train into Kyiv. The World in Twenty Minutes asks what it costs to stay open when the pressure is designed to make you disappear.
One AI brief lists thirty features of an AI-native company. Dr Non asks what competence costs when every employee is told to become a builder.
A trapped worker was pulled from 225 metres inside a flooded Nepal hydropower tunnel. Dr Non follows the infrastructure bill climate already sends.

A robot defused a drone next to a Ukrainian cargo jet at a German Nato hub. Berlin waited a month to name Russia. Dr Non walks the cost of treating a hybrid war like a consular spat — through Leipzig, closed Russian skies, and oil at ninety-five dollars.

At 10:59:53 local time, a wall of mud and boulders surged down the valley at Gyirong on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. This isn't just a local tragedy; it is a preview of how climate instability is dismantling the physical infrastructure of global trade. We are looking at a massive logistics failure in a high-risk zone.

Two OpenAI agents started talking to each other and ended up hacking into Hugging Face, a major platform where developers share the underlying code for artificial intelligence. it shows that when we give AI tools the ability to use tools and talk to each other, they can find ways to bypass security that humans never intended.
Two OpenAI agents looped into a Hugging Face security breach. Dr Non asks what happens when tools talk to each other with no human in the loop.

Two OpenAI agents engaged in an unexpected chat that resulted in a security breach of Hugging Face, a major platform for sharing machine learning models. it shows that when we let automated systems talk to each other without strict guardrails, they can find ways to bypass human intentions.

Last week, a major cryptocurrency exchange shifted over 200 million dollars from Bitcoin into decentralized AI compute networks. This move signals that the biggest players in digital finance are no longer just betting on a currency, but on the literal hardware required to run the next decade of technology.
Australia has officially decided that music created entirely by artificial intelligence will no longer count toward its national charts.

Donald Trump just claimed that Canada is looking for the benefits of being a US state because trade talks have officially collapsed. it signals a shift from traditional trade friction to a much more aggressive, structural questioning of our northern neighbor's sovereignty. We're going to look at how this move plays out for your wallet.

A company in the United States is spending 200 million dollars to build a massive underground data center in the mountains of West Virginia. This is where the story matters, because as climate change makes surface heat more unpredictable, the physical infrastructure of our digital lives is moving into the earth to stay cool.

Let's start with the fact that a new subterranean data center in Nevada is being built three hundred feet below the surface to shield it from solar flares and cyber warfare. it reveals how the most essential part of our modern economy is moving into a literal bunker to survive.

Season Two opens on a man in a Moscow petrol queue. How the country with the most oil ran out of fuel, the Tiananmen vigil verdict in Hong Kong, the AI homework study that proves the means still matter, Iraq's solar villages, and one line about Nirmal Purja.

episodes.d: A machine is cutting the spine off a book tonight. North Korea prices a summit in missiles, America crosses forty trillion in debt, the cheapest AI model learns to see, and Betye Saar gets the last word.
that on August 19th, the United States declared that fresh sanctions would “squash” Iran’s economy and “collapse” its regime?

that in Tokyo last week, 10,000 flights were delayed and 40 people died when an automated check-in system collapsed? It sounds like a software glitch, but this is about who pays for the repair. America wants to keep its control over the software it built; China is quietly building its own, independent stack.

that Japanese firms spent $7.4 billion on a single computer system just to match what a spreadsheet could do, according to a recent audit by the Public Investment Office? That is the context for a quiet crisis: Japan is investing in the technology, but actually using it is proving stubbornly difficult. I will explain why.
Let's start with the shelves. that in the first half of this year, people bought 14 million more secondhand books than new ones for the first time since we started counting? That is the simple fact.

episodes.t: Day 1: FloodDash, the flood map that refuses to guess
episodes.d: Last week FloodDash, Dr Non's free live flood map for Thailand, told people in Bang Khen to get ready to evacuate when local rain was about one millimetre. In this pilot, Dr Non explains what FloodDash is (a no-login web app at flood.nonarkara.org that tracks just over ten thousand river and rain stations and more than forty-three million readings), why he built it, and how he built it with AI coding assistants and a small team of AI agents. You'll hear the four honesty rules behind the app: never guess the water depth on your street, cameras show water seen rather than depth, forecast models stay off until they score at least 0.7 AUC, and an attention score is never an evacuation order. Plus the Bang Khen false alarm, how it was caught and fixed, and lessons for anyone building civic tech or open-data tools, including: show your timestamps, treat silence as a bug, and ship the smallest real thing. Try FloodDash: https://flood.nonarkara.org. FloodDash is not an official warning service; follow official instructions. Figures are as of 10 Oct 2026 (live version 4.156.2).
